pages.title: Table of Contents & Important Safety Information
pages.summary: This page presents the manual's Table of Contents, defines the warning symbols and their severity levels, and begins the General Safety section with eight numbered safety practices for operating the welder.
keyFacts: DANGER indicates a hazardous situation which, if not avoided, will result in death or serious injury.
WARNING indicates a hazardous situation which, if not avoided, could result in death or serious injury.
CAUTION indicates a hazardous situation which, if not avoided, could result in minor or moderate injury.
NOTICE/CAUTION addresses practices not related to personal injury.
Read all Safety warnings and instructions; failure to follow may result in electric shock, fire and/or serious injury.
Save all warnings and instructions for future reference.
Read and understand manufacturer's instructions, Material Safety Data Sheets (MSDS's), employer's Safety practices, and ANSI Z49.1 before use.
Keep out of reach of children; keep children and bystanders away while operating.
Place the welder on a stable location before use — if it falls while plugged in, severe injury, electric shock, or fire may result.
Do not overreach; keep proper footing and balance at all times.
Do not use a welder while tired or under the influence of drugs, alcohol or medication.
Avoid unintentional starting; make sure you are prepared to begin work before turning on the Welder.
Never leave the Welder unattended while energized — turn power off if you have to leave.
Item 57812; technical questions call 1-800-444-3353.

pages.title: Fume and Gas Safety / Arc Ray Safety
pages.summary: Safety page covering inhalation hazards from welding/plasma cutting fumes and arc ray hazards to eyes and skin, with protective measures and ventilation requirements.
keyFacts: INHALATION HAZARD: Welding and Plasma Cutting produce toxic fumes.
Exposure to welding/cutting exhaust fumes can increase risk of certain cancers, such as cancer of the larynx and lung cancer.

Diseases linked to exposure: Early onset of Parkinson's Disease, Heart disease, Ulcers, Damage to reproductive organs, Inflammation of the small intestine or stomach, Kidney damage, Respiratory diseases such as emphysema, bronchitis, or pneumonia.
Use natural or forced air ventilation and wear a respirator approved by NIOSH.
Do not use near degreasing or painting operations.
Keep head out of fumes; do not breathe exhaust fumes.
Use enough ventilation, exhaust at arc, or both; if engineering controls not feasible use an approved respirator.
Work in a confined area only if well-ventilated or while wearing an air-supplied respirator.
Follow OSHA guidelines for Permissible Exposure Limits (PEL's) and ACGIH Threshold Limit Values (TLV's) for fumes and gases.
ARC RAYS can injure eyes and burn skin.
Wear ANSI-approved welding eye protection with at least a number 10 shade lens rating.
Wear leather leggings, fire resistant shoes or boots; do not wear pants with cuffs, shirts with open pockets, or clothing that can catch molten metal or sparks.
Keep clothing free of grease, oil, solvents, or flammable substances; wear dry insulating gloves.
Wear an approved head covering to protect head and neck.
Wear an approved welding jacket or long sleeves to protect forearms from radiation burns.
When welding/cutting overhead or in confined spaces, wear flame resistant ear plugs or ear muffs.
Item 57812; technical questions 1-800-444-3353.

pages.title: Electrical Safety and Fire Safety
pages.summary: Page 4 covers electrical safety (electric shock hazards) and fire safety (arc and slag fire hazards) for the Vulcan OmniPro 220 welder. It lists numbered precautions for avoiding electric shock and preventing fires during welding operations.
keyFacts: ELECTRIC SHOCK can KILL.
Turn off, disconnect power, and discharge electrode to ground before setting down torch/electrode holder and before service.
Do not touch energized electrical parts; wear dry insulating gloves; do not touch electrode holder, electrode, welding torch, or welding wire with bare hand.
Do not wear wet or damaged gloves.
Connect to grounded, GFCI-protected power supply only.
Do not use near water or damp objects.
People with pacemakers should consult their physician(s) before use — electromagnetic fields near a heart pacemaker could cause interference or failure.
Do not expose welders to rain or wet conditions; water entering a welder increases risk of electric shock.
Do not abuse the cord; never use it for carrying, pulling or unplugging; keep cord away from heat, oil, sharp edges or moving parts.
Do not use outdoors.
Insulate yourself from the workpiece and ground using nonflammable dry insulating material, rubber mats, dry wood or plywood.
THIS WELDING MACHINE MUST BE CONNECTED TO POWER SOURCE IN ACCORDANCE WITH APPLICABLE ELECTRICAL CODES.
ARC AND SLAG can cause fire.
Clear away or protect flammable objects within a radius of 35 feet (10 meters) around the work area.
Keep ABC-type fire extinguisher near work area and know how to use it.
Maintain a safe working environment — well lit, free of obstructions, grease, oil, trash and debris.
Do not operate welders in atmospheres containing reactive or flammable liquids, gases, vapors, or dust.
Do not weld or cut on materials having combustible coating or internal structure without an approved hazard-elimination method.
Do not dispose of hot slag in containers holding combustible materials.
After welding, make a thorough examination for evidence of fire; smoke or flame may not be visible for some time.
Do not apply heat to a container that has held an unknown or combustible substance; clean and purge containers and vent closed containers/castings before preheating, welding, or cutting.
Designate a fire watch equipped with fire extinguisher during cutting and for at least one half hour after cutting is completed.
Item 57812; technical questions 1-800-444-3353.

pages.title: Welder Use and Care, Maintenance, and Gas Cylinder Safety
pages.summary: Safety instructions covering proper welder use and care, maintenance procedures, and gas-shielded welding cylinder safety. Emphasizes unplugging before maintenance and that cylinders can explode when damaged.
keyFacts: Do not use the welder if the switch does not turn it on and off; any welder that cannot be controlled with the switch is dangerous and must be repaired.
Disconnect the plug from the power source before making any adjustments, changing accessories, or storing welders.
Ensure the switch is in the off-position before connecting to power source or moving the welder.
Store idle welders out of the reach of children and untrained users.
Do not use the welder for pipe thawing.
Have your welder serviced by a qualified repair person using only identical replacement parts.
Maintain labels and nameplates; if unreadable or missing, contact Harbor Freight Tools for a replacement.
Unplug the Welder from its electrical outlet before any inspection, maintenance, or cleaning procedures.
WARNING: Cylinders can explode when damaged.
Do not weld on a pressurized or closed cylinder.
Do not allow an electrode holder, electrode, welding torch, or welding wire to touch the cylinder.
Keep cylinders away from any electrical circuits, including welding circuits.
Keep protective cap in place over the valve except when the cylinder is in use.
Use only correct gas shielding equipment designed specifically for the type of welding.
Protect gas cylinders from heat, being struck, physical damage, slag, flames, sparks, and arcs.
Use proper procedures to move cylinders.

pages.title: Grounding, Extension Cords, Replacement Cords & Symbology
pages.summary: Safety page covering proper grounding of the welder, prohibition of extension cords, replacement cord rules, and a symbology legend explaining icons and abbreviations used throughout the manual.
keyFacts: WARNING: To prevent electric shock and death from incorrect grounding wire connection, check with a qualified electrician if in doubt whether the outlet is properly grounded.
Do not use the welder if the power cord or plug is damaged; have it repaired by a service facility before use.
If the plug will not fit the outlet, have a proper outlet installed by a qualified electrician; do not use adapter plugs.
The green wire inside the cord connects to the grounding system in the welder and must be the only wire connected to the welder's grounding system.
The green wire must never be attached to an electrically 'live' terminal; never leave the grounding wire disconnected or modify either Power Cord Plug.

Make sure the tool is connected to an outlet having the same configuration as the plug; reconnection for a different circuit type should be made by qualified service personnel and comply with local codes.
Do not use an extension cord on this welder.
Use only one of the supplied power cords for this welder or an identical replacement cord.
Do not install a thinner or longer cord on this welder.
Do not patch cords of any length together; patches may allow moisture to penetrate the insulation, resulting in electric shock.
VAC = Volts Alternating Current.
A = Amperes.
OCV = Open Circuit Voltage.
KVA = Kilovolt Amperes (Volts / 1000 * Amperes).
IPM = Inches Per Minute.
AWG = American Wire Gauge.

pages.title: Wire Spool Installation / Wire Setup
pages.summary: Instructions for installing a 1-2 lb wire spool on the Vulcan welder, including powering off and unplugging, opening the door, mounting the spool so it unwinds clockwise, and securing it with the spacer and wingnut.
keyFacts: To prevent serious injury from accidental operation: Turn the Power Switch off and unplug the Welder before setup.
Remove the protective foam and cardboard from the Welder before setup.
Step 1: Turn the Power Switch OFF and unplug the Welder before proceeding.
Step 2: Pull up on the Door Latch, then open the Door.
Step 3 (1-2 Pound Wire Spool Installation): Remove the Wingnut and Spacer. If replacing a Spool, remove the old Spool and all remaining wire from the liners.
Step 4: Place the new Wire Spool over the Spool Spindle and against the Spool Brake Pad. To prevent wire feed problems, set the Spool so that it will unwind clockwise.
Step 5: Replace the Spacer over the Spool Spindle and secure Spool in place with the Wingnut.
Notice: If Wire Spool can spin freely, Wingnut is too loose. This will cause the welding wire to unravel and unspool which can cause tangling and feeding problems.
Supports 1-2 lb wire spools.
Item 57812. Technical questions: 1-800-444-3353.

pages.summary: Explains duty cycle limits at 120VAC and 240VAC, the internal thermal protection system, and how to prepare and clamp workpieces including ground cable connection based on welding polarity.
keyFacts: Duty Cycle defines the number of minutes within a 10 minute period during which the welder can produce a particular welding current without overheating.
120VAC rating: 40% use at 100A for 10 continuous minutes (4 minutes welding, 6 minutes resting).
120VAC: 100% continuous use at 75A.
240VAC rating: 25% use at 200A for 10 continuous minutes (2-1/2 minutes welding, 7-1/2 minutes resting).
240VAC: 100% continuous use at 115A.
Example: a 40% duty cycle welder at 100A must rest at least 6 minutes after every 4 minutes of continuous welding.
Failure to observe duty cycle limits can over-stress the welder's power generation system causing premature failure.
Welder has internal thermal protection that automatically shuts down and shows a warning screen in the LCD Display when overheated; it returns to service after cooling off.
If overheating occurs, rest the MIG Gun on an electrically non-conductive, heat-proof surface (such as a concrete slab), well clear of the ground clamp.
Allow the Welder to cool with the Power Switch ON so the internal Fan helps cool it.
Make practice welds on scrap of the same thickness before welding anything of value.
Clean weld surfaces thoroughly with a wire brush or angle grinder; no rust, paint, oil, or other materials — only bare metal.
Clamp Ground Cable to bare metal on the workpiece near the weld area or to a metal work bench where the workpiece is clamped.
Edges of thicker workpieces may need to be chamfered (beveled) to allow proper weld penetration.

Notice: When welding equipment on a vehicle, disconnect the vehicle battery power from both the positive connection and the ground before welding to prevent damage from high voltage and high frequency bursts.
Ground connection depends on desired welding polarity.

pages.title: Basic Wire Welding Technique
pages.summary: Explains fundamental MIG/wire welding techniques including stringer vs weave beads, MIG gun angle for butt and fillet welds, push angle vs drag angle for solid vs flux-cored wire, and maintaining proper Contact Tip to Work Distance (CTWD).
keyFacts: Press and hold the Trigger and contact the area to be welded with electrode wire to ignite the arc.
Stringer bead: draw the wire in a steady straight line for a narrow weld.
Weave bead: draw the wire back and forth across the joint for a wider weld; takes practice.
Direct the welding wire straight into the joint at 90° (straight up and down) for butt (end to end) welds.
Use a 45° angle for fillet (T-shaped) welds.
For MIG welding with solid wire and shielding gas, tilt the MIG Gun so wire is angled 0–15° away from the direction of travel — this is the push angle.
For flux-cored wire without shielding gas, tilt the MIG Gun so wire is angled 0–15° in the direction you are welding — this is the drag angle.
Contact Tip should remain within 1/2" of the work surface; this distance is called CTWD (Contact Tip to Work Distance).
CTWD should be up to 1/2".

pages.title: Overheating Warning, Duty Cycle, and Welder Shutdown Procedure
pages.summary: Explains the auto-shutdown warning screen when the welder overheats, how to cool the unit, and the finishing steps to complete welding. Provides the duty-cycle matrix for 120VAC and 240VAC operation and the shutdown/respool procedure.
keyFacts: If the Welder is used too long, a warning screen appears in the LCD Display and the unit automatically shuts down.
The Welder automatically returns to service after cooling off.
If overheating occurs, rest the MIG Gun on an electrically non-conductive, heat-proof surface (concrete slab) away from the ground clamp.
Allow the Welder to cool with the Power Switch ON so the internal Fan helps cool the Welder.
Use shorter welding periods and longer rest periods to prevent needless wear.
CAUTION! Weld will be hot, do not touch.
120VAC: 40% duty cycle Use at 100A — 4 Minutes Welding / 6 Minutes Resting per 10 continuous minutes.
120VAC: 100% Continuous Use at 75A.
240VAC: 25% duty cycle Use at 200A — 2-1/2 Minutes Welding / 7-1/2 Minutes Resting per 10 continuous minutes.
240VAC: 100% Continuous Use at 115A.
When welding is complete, set MIG Gun on a heat-proof, electrically non-conductive surface and turn the Power Switch OFF.
Allow Welder to cool down, then unplug the Power Cord.
Remove Ground Clamp from workpiece and disconnect MIG Gun.
Respool wire by clipping wire, removing gas nozzle/contact tip, releasing Idler Arm on Wire Feed mechanism, and rotating Wire Spool counterclockwise.
Hold wire securely while respooling because the wire end tends to quickly unravel once it clears the wire feeder.
MIG ONLY: Close shielding gas cylinder valve securely, remove Regulator and replace cap, disconnect Gas Hose, store and secure gas cylinder.
Warning screen fault conditions: Duty Cycle Exceeded, Low Voltage Input, High Voltage Input.
Item 57812; Page 23; technical questions 1-800-444-3353.

pages.summary: Instructions for sharpening a tungsten electrode on a dedicated fine grit grinding wheel and for assembling the TIG torch components (collet, collet body, ceramic nozzle, back cap). Both the electrode and TIG torch are sold separately.
keyFacts: WARNING: Some electrodes may have materials added that are hazardous to breathe — wear a respirator and ANSI-approved safety goggles when grinding an electrode.
Dedicate a fine grit grinding wheel exclusively to electrode grinding to avoid electrode contamination.
Shut off the welder and let electrode and torch cool before handling.
Remove electrode from the FRONT of the torch — pulling from the rear will damage the collet and create burrs on the electrode.
Grinding direction must be parallel to the length of the electrode.
The conical portion of the ideal tip will be 2-1/2 times as long as the electrode diameter.
Re-insert electrode into collet with tip protruding 1/8"-1/4" beyond the ceramic nozzle, then re-tighten the back cap.
Electrode should protrude 1/8" to 1/4" beyond the ceramic nozzle when locked with the back cap.
Consult the Settings Chart on top of the welder to determine proper tungsten electrode size for material thickness.
Match collet and collet body sizes to the tungsten electrode size.

Torch assembly order: thread collet body into front of torch, thread ceramic nozzle onto collet body, insert collet into back of torch and into collet body, insert tungsten electrode into collet from front.

pages.title: Duty Cycle (Duration of Use) & Setting Up the Weld
pages.summary: Explains the duty cycle concept and gives TIG and Stick rated duty-cycle matrices for the Vulcan OmniPro 220 at 240VAC and 120VAC. Also covers preparing and clamping workpieces and ground cable placement for welding.
keyFacts: Duty cycle = number of minutes within a 10-minute period a welder can produce a given current without overheating.
Example: a 40% duty cycle at 125A requires at least 6 minutes rest after every 4 minutes of continuous welding.
Welder has internal thermal protection that automatically shuts down and shows a warning screen in the LCD display when overheated; returns to service after cooling off.
When overheated, rest the TIG torch or electrode holder on an electrically non-conductive, heat-proof surface (such as a concrete slab), well clear of the ground clamp.
Allow the welder to cool with the Power Switch ON so the internal fan helps cool the welder.
TIG 240VAC: 30% use at 175A (3 min welding / 7 min resting for 10 continuous minutes); 100% continuous use at 105A.
TIG 120VAC: 40% use at 125A (4 min welding / 6 min resting for 10 continuous minutes); 100% continuous use at 90A.
Stick 240VAC: 25% use at 175A (2-1/2 min welding / 7-1/2 min resting for 10 continuous minutes); 100% continuous use at 100A.
Stick 120VAC: 40% use at 80A (4 min welding / 6 min resting for 10 continuous minutes); 100% continuous use at 60A.
Clean weld surfaces thoroughly with a wire brush or angle grinder; no rust, paint, oil, or other materials — only bare metal.
Edges of thicker workpieces may need chamfering (beveling) to allow proper weld penetration.
Clamp Ground Cable to bare metal on the workpiece near the weld area, or to the metal work bench where the workpiece is clamped.
NOTICE: When welding equipment on a vehicle, disconnect vehicle battery power from both positive connection and ground before welding to prevent damage from high voltage and high frequency bursts.

pages.title: Welding Tips: Strike Test and Cleaning the Weld
pages.summary: This page explains how to evaluate weld quality by examining a cooled weld and performing a destructive strike test on scrap, plus how to safely clean a weld of slag using a chipping hammer and wire brush.
keyFacts: Examine a weld's appearance after it has cooled and the slag has been removed to assess technique.
NOTICE: TIG welding is a complicated process requiring experience and skill; training beyond this manual is required to TIG weld properly.
After practice welding a couple of beads, STOP and examine your weld using the guidelines.
Strike Test: perform a test weld on a PIECE OF SCRAP; WEAR ANSI-APPROVED SAFETY GOGGLES during the procedure.
CAUTION! The strike test WILL damage the weld it is performed on; it is ONLY an indicator of weld technique and is not intended to test working welds.
Strike test step 1: After two scraps have been welded together and the weld has cooled, clamp one scrap in a sturdy vise.
Strike test step 2: Stay clear from underneath while you strike the opposite scrap with a heavy hammer, preferably a dead-blow hammer.
Strike test step 3: A GOOD WELD will deform but not break; a POOR WELD will be brittle and snap at the weld.
GOOD WELD bends and is not brittle; POOR WELD snaps or cracks.
WARNING - TO PREVENT SERIOUS INJURY: Continue to wear ANSI-approved safety goggles and protective wear when cleaning a weld; sparks or chips may fly.
Cleaning step 1: A weld from flux-cored wire welding or stick welding will be covered by slag; use a chipping hammer to knock this off. Be careful not to damage the weld or base material.
Cleaning step 2: Use a wire brush to further clean the weld, or use an angle grinder (sold separately) to shape the weld.

To reduce workpiece heat and limit penetration (weld THINNER workpieces): (e) decrease weld current, (f) increase travel speed, (g) use slower wire feed, (h) use longer CTWD.
CTWD = Contact Tip to Work Distance.

Voltage Too High or Wire Feed Too Fast — TO CORRECT: decrease output voltage OR decrease wire feed speed.
Travel Speed Too Fast — TO CORRECT: travel slower.
Travel Speed Too Slow — TO CORRECT: travel faster.
CTWD Too Long or Wrong Polarity — TO CORRECT: check polarity and maintain less than 1/2" CTWD.

pages.title: Weld Diagnosis: Penetration, Bend at Joint, Slag, and Adhesion Problems
pages.summary: This troubleshooting page teaches how to diagnose and correct wire-weld defects related to workpiece heat control and joint quality. It covers excess/proper/inadequate penetration, bend at joint, slag coating on flux-cored welds, and welds not adhering properly, each with profile-view diagrams and causes/solutions.
keyFacts: Excess penetration/burn-through: weld droops on top and underneath, or falls through entirely making a hole.
Proper penetration: weld is visible underneath and bulges slightly on top.
Inadequate penetration: weld does not penetrate the joint fully, just on the surface.
Excess penetration solutions: reduce wire feed speed, decrease weld current, increase travel speed, keep travel speed steady, reduce excessive material at weld.

Inadequate penetration solutions: maintain 1/2" or less CTWD (contact tip to work distance), keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle, hold MIG gun at proper angles, reduce travel speed, increase weld current, bevel thick workpieces and allow slight gap and weld in several passes, increase wire feed speed.
Bend at joint causes: improper clamping (clamp securely, make tack welds) and excessive heat (weld small portion and cool, increase travel speed, reduce wire feed speed).
Slag is a necessary part of a flux-cored wire weld; it shields the weld from impurities. Clean off slag with a Chipping Hammer and Wire Brush after welding.
Gas-shielded MIG welds are protected by shielding gas and do not need slag to protect them.
Weld not adhering: gaps present between weld and previous bead or between weld and workpiece.

Adhesion solutions: place stringer bead correctly, adjust workpiece/weld angle, pause briefly at sides during weave bead, keep arc on leading edge, hold MIG gun at proper angles, increase current and wire feed speed, clean workpiece to bare metal, widen groove or increase bevel if gap too narrow.

pages.title: Wire Weld Troubleshooting — Porosity, Excessive Spatter, Crooked/Wavy Bead, Burn-Through
pages.summary: Weld-defect diagnosis page for wire (MIG/flux-cored) welding, showing top-view bead appearance for four common defects along with possible causes and solutions. Covers porosity, excessive spatter, crooked/wavy beads, and burn-through.
keyFacts: Porosity appears as small cavities or holes in the bead.

Porosity causes/solutions: incorrect polarity (check polarity set correctly for type of welding); insufficient shielding gas (MIG only) - increase flow, clean nozzle, maintain proper CTWD; incorrect shielding gas (MIG only) - use gas recommended by wire supplier; dirty workpiece or welding wire - clean to bare metal, free of oil/coatings/residues; inconsistent travel speed - maintain steady travel speed; CTWD too long - reduce CTWD.
Excessive Spatter: fine spatter is normal; spatter that is grainy and large is a problem.

Excessive Spatter causes/solutions: dirty workpiece or welding wire - clean to bare metal, free of oil/coatings/residues; incorrect polarity - check polarity set correctly; insufficient shielding gas (MIG only) - increase flow, clean nozzle, maintain proper CTWD; wire feeding too fast - reduce wire feed speed; CTWD too long - reduce CTWD.
Crooked/Wavy Bead causes/solutions: inaccurate welding - use two hands or rest hand on steady surface; inconsistent travel speed - maintain steady travel speed; CTWD too long - reduce CTWD.
Burn-Through: base material melts away, leaving a hole in the weld.

Burn-Through causes/solutions: workpiece overheating - reduce current and/or wire feed speed; travel speed too slow - increase travel speed and keep steady; excessive material at weld - reduce wire feed speed.
CTWD = Contact Tip to Work Distance; reducing it helps several defects.
Item 57812; technical questions 1-800-444-3353; Page 37.

pages.summary: This page teaches how to diagnose stick (SMAW) welds by evaluating workpiece heat and weld penetration, and provides example weld bead photos showing common defects and their corrections. keyFacts: Inadequate penetration = 'Not hot enough'; Proper penetration = 'Ideal heat'; Excess penetration or burn-through = 'Too hot'.
To increase workpiece heat and increase penetration (to weld THICKER workpieces properly): a. Increase current; b. Weld more slowly.
To reduce workpiece heat and limit penetration (to weld THINNER workpieces properly): c. Decrease current; d. Weld more quickly.
CLEAN WELDS FIRST! — Stick welds will have a coat of slag over them until cleaned.

Current Too High — TO CORRECT: Decrease the current.
Weld Speed Too Fast — TO CORRECT: Weld slower.
Weld Speed Too Slow — TO CORRECT: Weld faster.
Arc Length Too Short — TO CORRECT: Increase distance.
Arc Length Too Long — TO CORRECT: Decrease distance.

pages.summary: This troubleshooting page teaches how to diagnose stick weld penetration problems (excess/burn-through, proper, inadequate), welds not adhering properly, and bending at the joint, with profile-view illustrations and causes/solutions for each.
keyFacts: Proper penetration: weld is visible underneath and bulges slightly on top.
Excess penetration or burn-through: weld droops on top and underneath or falls through entirely, making a hole.
Inadequate penetration: weld does not contact the joint fully, just on the surface.
Excess penetration cause 1 - Workpiece overheating: reduce current.
Excess penetration cause 2 - Welding speed too slow: increase welding speed and keep it steady.
Inadequate penetration cause 1 - Incorrect welding technique: keep arc on leading edge of weld puddle, hold torch at proper angles.
Inadequate penetration cause 2 - Insufficient weld heat: slow down so fill material has time to melt into the weld location, increase current.
Inadequate penetration cause 3 - Workpieces too thick/close: bevel thick workpieces, allow slight gap, weld in several passes.
Inadequate penetration cause 4 - Insufficient weld material: increase amount of fill material.
Weld not adhering: gaps present between weld and previous bead or between weld and workpiece.

Not adhering cause 1 - Incorrect welding technique: place stringer bead at correct place in joint, adjust workpiece position or weld angle, keep arc on leading edge of puddle, hold electrode and fill material at proper angles.
Not adhering cause 2 - Insufficient weld heat: increase current.
Not adhering cause 3 - Dirty workpiece: clean workpiece down to bare metal.
Not adhering cause 4 - Insufficient weld material: increase amount of fill material.
Not adhering cause 5 - Distance between workpieces too large: decrease distance and increase bevel.
Bend at joint cause 1 - Improper clamping: clamp workpieces securely, make tack welds to hold workpieces.
Bend at joint cause 2 - Excessive heat: weld a small portion and allow to cool before proceeding, increase weld speed.

pages.title: MIG Gun Nozzle & Contact Tip Cleaning; Replacing the LCD Screen Cover
pages.summary: Maintenance page covering general inspection before/after each use, step-by-step MIG gun nozzle and contact tip inspection and cleaning, and the procedure for replacing the LCD screen cover on the display.
keyFacts: WARNING: To prevent serious injury, fire and burns — Unplug the Welder, rest the tool on a heat-proof, electrically non-conductive surface, and allow all parts of the Welder to cool thoroughly before service.

BEFORE EACH USE, inspect general condition: check for loose hardware, misalignment or binding of moving parts, damaged cord/electrical wiring, frayed or damaged cables, cracked or broken parts, and any other unsafe condition.
PERIODICALLY, have a qualified technician remove the Rear Panel and use compressed air to blow out all dust from the interior.
AFTER EVERY USE, store in a clean and dry location.
For optimal MIG/Flux-Cored wire weld quality, clean and inspect the MIG Gun Contact Tip and Nozzle before each use.
MIG Gun cleaning step 1: Make sure the entire MIG Gun is completely cool and the Power Cord is unplugged from the electrical outlet before proceeding.
Step 2: Pull the Nozzle to remove it.
Step 3: Scrub the interior of the Nozzle clean with a wire brush.
Step 4: Examine the end of the Nozzle — it should be flat and even; if uneven, chipped, melted, cracked, or otherwise damaged, the Nozzle should be replaced.
Step 5: Unscrew the Contact Tip counterclockwise and slide it off the welding wire to remove.
Step 6: Scrub the outside of the Tip clean with a wire brush; clean the inside with a tip cleaner (sold separately); check the Tip is the proper type for the wire size used.
Step 7: Examine the hole at the end of the Contact Tip — it should be an even circle, not oblong or bulged.
Step 8: If problems are noted, replace the Contact Tip; select a new Tip of the correct size for the welding wire used.
Step 9: Reinstall the Tip and securely reinstall the Nozzle.
LCD Screen Cover replacement step 1: Carefully pry frame off of Display (22) by inserting a flathead screwdriver (sold separately) into one of the side slots.
LCD step 2: Insert a new Screen Cover (17) into Screen Frame (18) with the gap facing downward.
LCD step 3: Insert frame back into slot on Display with the top end placed in first.
Part numbers referenced: Display (22), Screen Cover (17), Screen Frame (18).
Item 57812; technical questions 1-800-444-3353.

pages.title: Troubleshooting - MIG / Flux-Cored Welding
pages.summary: A troubleshooting table for MIG/Flux-Cored welding problems, listing symptoms, possible causes, and likely solutions covering wire feed issues, bird's nesting, wire stoppage, unstable arc, and weak arc strength.
keyFacts: IMPORTANT: Shut off the Welder, disconnect it from power, and discharge the MIG Gun to ground before adjusting, cleaning, or repairing the unit.
DCEP is used for MIG welding and DCEN is used for Flux-Cored self-shielded welding.
Increase/adjust wire feed pressure per step 27 on page 17.
Feed Roller instructions are on page 12; correct roll size can be flipped.
Gun Cable Connector insertion follows steps 13 and 14 on page 13.
MIG Gun Cable Connector must be fully inserted into Wire Feed mechanism with no O-Rings exposed.
Loosen Feed Tensioner so it applies only enough pressure to prevent continued spinning after the Gun Trigger is released.
Do not use an extension cord on this Welder; use only supplied power cords or an identical replacement cord.
Gas flow rate should be set according to the Settings Chart.
Switch current to proper setting for metal thickness for weak arc strength.
Follow all safety precautions whenever diagnosing or servicing the equipment.

rows: Wire Feed Motor Runs but Wire Does Not Feed Properly
1. Insufficient wire feed pressure. 2. Incorrect wire feed roller size. 3. Damaged MIG Gun, cable, or liner assembly. 4. Feed Tensioner is too tight.

1. Increase wire feed pressure properly. Follow step 27 on page 17. 2. Flip roll to correct size. Follow the Feed Roller instructions on page 12. 3. Have a qualified technician inspect these parts and replace as necessary. 4. Loosen Feed Tensioner so it applies only enough pressure to prevent continued spinning after the Gun Trigger is released.
Wire Creates a Bird's Nest During Operation
1. Excess wire feed pressure. 2. Incorrect Contact Tip size. 3. MIG Gun Cable Connector not fully inserted into Wire Feed mechanism. 4. Damaged liner.

1. Adjust wire feed pressure properly. Follow step 27 on page 17. 2. Replace with the proper tip for wire used. 3. Insert Gun Cable Connector properly. Follow steps 13 and 14 on page 13. 4. Have a qualified technician inspect and repair/replace as necessary.

1. Gun cable is severely bent and Wire Feed mechanism cannot feed wire. 2. Gun liner is clogged or worn. 3. Gun liner is too small for welding wire being used. 4. Wire is tangled on the spool. 5. Wire is not making contact with Feed Rollers. 6. Feed Roller is not making enough contact with wire or is crushing flux-cored wire.

keyFacts: IMPORTANT! Identify your input voltage: do you have 120 volt or 240 volt?
Flux-Cored/FCAW: Low skill level, No-Gas Required, welds Steel and Stainless Steel, thickness 18 Gauge to 5/16"
MIG/GMAW: Low skill level, Gas Required (indoor welding recommended), welds Steel, Stainless Steel, Aluminum (spool gun required), thickness 22 Gauge to 3/8"
Stick/SMAW: Moderate skill level, No-Gas Required, welds Steel, Stainless Steel, Castings, thickness 10 Gauge to 1/2"

Steel, Stainless Steel, Chrome Moly require DC TIG
Aluminum, Magnesium Alloys require AC TIG
Aluminum with MIG requires a spool gun
Duty Cycle definition: the number of minutes, within a 10-minute period, a welding process can produce the specified welding current without overheating
Duty Cycle Example: 165A @ 30% Duty Cycle = 3 Minutes Welding, 7 Minutes Resting
MIG uses solid wire, uses shielding gas, and produces clean welds with minimal spatter
Flux-Cored uses cored wire, welds over mill scale and rust, requires minimal surface prep, can be used outdoors in windy conditions, deep weld penetration, handles material gaps well
MIG is best for thin materials like sheet metal
